title: Values and types
summary: Numbers, text and booleans, how + treats them, and how typeof names a value's type.

concepts.title: Finding a value's type with typeof

misconceptions.description: Believes + and - are done before * and /, or that every operator works strictly from left to right.
Believes / always gives a whole number, rounding down or to the nearest integer.
Believes % tells how many times a number fits into another instead of what is left over.
Reads the value a variable has at a different moment than the one asked about, such as the start or the end of the program.
Believes + always does arithmetic, so mixing a number with text gives a sum or NaN.
Believes trim removes spaces from only one end of the text.
Believes a string method has no visible effect unless its result is stored, so ignores the new text it returns.
Believes a boolean joins text as a number or disappears, instead of becoming the word true or false.
Treats null and undefined as the same value, or expects typeof to answer null for them.

conceptCard.title: Numbers and arithmetic
conceptCard.body: JavaScript has one kind of number, with or without decimals. The signs + - * / work as in maths, and * and / go before + and -. The % sign gives the leftover after dividing. A let line stores a value under a name, and a later line can replace it.

conceptCard.title: Strings and joining text
conceptCard.body: Text goes between quotation marks. Joining texts with + makes one longer text. If one side of + is text, the other side becomes text too. The length property counts the characters. A method such as toUpperCase() is called after a dot and returns new text.

conceptCard.title: Booleans: true and false
conceptCard.body: A boolean is either true or false, written without quotation marks. It is a value, not text, but it prints as the word true or false. Joined to text, a boolean becomes that word. A variable can hold one.

lessons.title: Finding a value's type with typeof

conceptCard.title: Finding a value's type with typeof
conceptCard.body: typeof gives the type of a value as text, such as number, string or boolean. Quotation marks make digits a string. Two values are odd: undefined has its own type, and null reports object.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. 2 * 3 is done first, giving 6, and then 5 + 6 + 1 is 12.
You worked from left to right: 5 + 2 is 7, then 7 * 3 is 21, plus 1. Multiplication goes before addition.
You added the left part and the right part first. The * sign binds its two neighbours before any + does.

items.explanation: Multiplication happens before addition, whatever the order on the line. So 2 * 3 is 6 first, and then 5 + 6 + 1 gives 12.
hints: Look at the * sign in the middle of the sum.
Multiplication is done before addition and subtraction.
Work out 2 * 3 first, then add the rest from left to right.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. Division is exact, so the result has a fraction.
You dropped the fraction. The / sign does not round down; the decimal part stays in the result.
You rounded to the nearest whole number. The / sign never rounds; it gives the exact value.

items.explanation: The / sign divides exactly. 9 divided by 2 is 4.5, and JavaScript keeps the fraction. Numbers in JavaScript can have decimals.
hints: Look at what / does to the two numbers.
Division in JavaScript keeps the fractional part.
9 does not split evenly by 2; half of it is between 4 and 5.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: What value does tray hold right after line 2 has run?

options.feedback: Right. Line 2 replaced 12 with 12 / 4, and line 3 has not run yet.
That is the value at the end of the program. The question stops after line 2, before line 3 adds 5.
That is the value after line 1. Line 2 has run and replaced it with the result of the division.

items.explanation: Line 1 stores 12. Line 2 divides the stored value by 4 and stores the result, so tray is 3 at that moment. Line 3 changes it later, to 8.
hints: Follow the lines in order and stop after line 2.
A variable keeps its value until a later line replaces it.
Divide 12 by 4 and ignore line 3 for now.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints the remainder of 17 divided by 5.

options.feedback: Right. 17 % 5 is 2, the leftover after taking 5 out of 17 three times.
This prints 3.4, the exact quotient, not the leftover.
This multiplies, so the program prints 85.
This subtracts once, so the program prints 12.

items.explanation: The % sign gives what is left over after dividing. 5 fits into 17 three times, which uses 15, and 2 is left over.
hints: Look at the sign between 17 and 5.
One sign gives the leftover after a division.
Work out 17 / 5 first: 5 fits three whole times. The blank gives what is left after that.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 42, 2.5, 2 and 8, one per line.
items.explanation: Each line prints one number. 7 * 6 is 42, 20 / 8 is 2.5, 10 % 4 is 2 and 2 ** 3 is 8. The output order is the order of the lines.
hints: Work out what each line prints before you move it.
** raises a number to a power, and % gives a remainder.
Start with the line that prints the biggest number.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Which statement explains the two lines this program prints?

options.text: / gives the exact result with its fraction, and % gives the leftover after dividing.
options.feedback: Right. 10 / 4 is 2.5, and 10 % 4 is 2 because two whole 4s leave 2.

options.text: / gives a whole number, and % tells you how many times 4 fits into 10.
options.feedback: Run line 1 by hand: 10 / 4 does not print a whole number, so the first half cannot be right.

options.text: / gives the exact result, and % gives how many times 4 fits into 10.
options.feedback: Check the second half against line 2: if % counted how many 4s fit into 10, would it print what line 2 prints?

items.explanation: The / sign divides exactly and keeps the fraction, so 10 / 4 is 2.5. The % sign gives the leftover: 4 fits twice into 10, which uses 8, and 2 is left.
hints: Run each line by hand and compare the two results.
One sign keeps the fraction; the other keeps the leftover.
The leftover is what remains after taking out as many whole 4s as possible.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. The text "7" makes + join the two values instead of adding them.
You added the numbers. The quotation marks make 7 text, and + then joins instead of adding.
JavaScript does not fail here. A + with text on one side simply joins the two values.

items.explanation: When one side of + is text, + joins instead of adding. The number 4 turns into the text 4 and the two pieces are glued together as 47.
hints: Look at the quotation marks around the 7.
A + with text on one side joins the two pieces.
The result looks like two digits side by side.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. Both ends lose their spaces before the ! is joined on.
You removed only the spaces at the start. The trim method cleans both ends of the text.
You ignored the text trim returns. The method does not change the original, but its result is what gets joined with the !.

items.explanation: The trim method returns new text without the spaces at the start and at the end. So the text becomes tea, and the ! is joined on the end.
hints: Look at the spaces around tea.
trim removes spaces from both ends of text.
Remove the spaces, then add the ! to what is left.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: What does tag hold right after line 2 has run?

options.feedback: Right. Line 2 joined c onto ab, and line 3 has not run yet.
That is the value at the end of the program. The question stops after line 2, before line 3 doubles the text.
That is the value after line 1. Line 2 has run and replaced it with the joined text.

items.explanation: Line 1 stores ab. Line 2 joins c on the end and stores abc. Line 3 then joins that text to itself, so the final value is abcabc.
hints: Follow the lines in order and stop after line 2.
A + between two texts joins them into one text.
Add c to the right end of ab.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

Right. This method turns every letter into a small letter.

hints: Compare the capital letters in the output with the text in the code.
One method makes capitals and one makes small letters.
The first line needs capitals; the second needs small letters.

items.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints a short letter: greeting, order line, thanks.
items.explanation: Each line prints one text, and the output follows the order of the lines. The greeting comes first, then the order line with the number joined in, then the thanks.

A greeting comes before the rest of a letter.
The thanks line ends the letter.

items.prompt: Write an expression that gives the number of characters in title, spaces included.
items.explanation: Every text has a length property that counts all its characters, spaces included. Reading title.length gives that count without changing the text.
hints: You need a property of the text, not a method call.
A text keeps its character count in a built-in property.
Write the variable name, a dot, then the property name.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

A boolean does not turn into a number when it is joined to text. It becomes a word.
The boolean does not vanish when it is joined. Its word is added after the dash.

A variable can hold a boolean, and a boolean prints as a word.
Line 2 joins the word to a label, and line 3 prints it alone.

A boolean does not become a number when it is joined to text. It becomes the word.
False does not disappear when it is joined. It becomes the word false.

This joins the word false, so the program prints door: false.
A number joins as its digits, so the program prints door: 1.

items.prompt: Which statement explains the two lines this program prints?

options.text: Without quotes, true is a boolean value; with quotes it is text. Both print the word true.
options.feedback: Right. They are different kinds of value that happen to print the same word.

options.text: Without quotes, true is the number 1, so the first line prints 1.
options.feedback: A boolean is not a number. It prints as the word true, just like the text does.

options.text: Only the quoted line prints a word, because a boolean prints nothing on its own.
options.feedback: A boolean prints on its own. It shows as the word true or false.

items.explanation: Written without quotation marks, true is a boolean value. In quotation marks it is ordinary text. They are different kinds of value, but both print as the word true.
hints: Compare the two lines, one with quotation marks and one without.
Quotation marks make text; a boolean is written bare.
Both lines print the same word, but they are not the same kind of value.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. undefined is its own type, and typeof names it undefined.
null is a different value. typeof undefined does not give null.
undefined is not an object. It has a type of its own.

items.explanation: undefined is a value of its own, and it is the only value of its own type. So typeof gives the text undefined.
hints: Look at the word after typeof.
typeof gives the name of a value's type as text.
Ask whether undefined belongs to a type that other values share.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. This is a known quirk: typeof null gives object.
It seems logical, but typeof has no null answer. The quirk is that null reports object.
null and undefined are different values, and typeof does not mix them up.

items.explanation: typeof null gives object. This is an old mistake in JavaScript that was never fixed, because fixing it would break old programs. null is not an object.
hints: Look at the value after typeof.
null is a special case that surprises many people.
The result is a word you would also expect for a list or a record, not for a single plain value.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: What does label hold right after line 2 has run?

hints: Follow the lines in order and stop after line 2.
typeof gives the type of the value the variable holds at that moment.

items.prompt: Write an expression that gives the type of price, a colon, a space, then the value itself. For 4.5 it gives "number: 4.5".
items.explanation: typeof price gives the type name. Joining it to ": " and then to price builds the text. typeof binds tighter than +, so it applies to price alone.
hints: You need three pieces joined with +.
typeof gives the type name of a value as text, and + joins texts together.
The type name goes first and the value itself goes last, with a colon and a space between them.
